title: Software delivery: Speed cannot define performance alone
desc: Balances delivery speed, reliability, value and working conditions, using archetypes descriptively rather than attributing outcomes causally to AI.

kps.k: Software delivery performance requires a joint assessment of speed, reliability, value and working conditions.
kps.d: The 2025 DORA State of AI-assisted Software Development Report uses survey-based cluster analysis to identify seven team profiles. It argues that tracking throughput and instability reveals changes in delivery but cannot distinguish underlying constraints such as technical debt, inefficient processes or burnout. Its analysis therefore includes product and team performance, individual effectiveness, valuable work, friction and burnout. The substantive proposition is that delivery metrics alone cannot diagnose organisational performance.

kps.k: The report challenges an inevitable speed–stability trade-off, without treating speed as sufficient for success.
kps.d: DORA reports that its Pragmatic performers and Harmonious high-achiever profiles, together representing nearly 40% of survey respondents, combine strong throughput with stability. It presents these profiles as evidence that fast, reliable delivery exists in practice and as a reference for improvement, while acknowledging the difficulty of achieving it. Conversely, the Stable and methodical profile combines lower throughput with positive quality and value indicators and low burnout and friction. The disagreement here is with a presumed trade-off, not between competing sources in the supplied material.

kps.k: Different performance constraints call for different interventions rather than a uniform push to deliver faster.
kps.d: DORA distinguishes foundational process and environmental gaps from legacy-system instability that erodes the value of regular updates. Its Constrained by process profile, comprising 17% of respondents, combines stable systems with inefficient workflows, high burnout and limited impact. Its High impact, low cadence profile, comprising 7%, combines strong product outcomes with low throughput and high instability, which the report warns could threaten long-term reliability. The practical implication is to identify whether technical foundations, workflow design or operational reliability constrain a team before choosing an intervention.

kps.k: Similar delivery results can conceal materially different employee experiences.
kps.d: Both leading delivery profiles achieve speed and stability, but Pragmatic performers report average burnout and friction, whereas Harmonious high-achievers report low levels of both alongside positive product outcomes. DORA interprets the former as functional but potentially lacking strong engagement drivers and the latter as sustainable high performance. This distinction supports monitoring working conditions separately rather than assuming that strong output establishes team health.

kps.k: The archetypes offer descriptive reference points, not definitive diagnoses or evidence of AI's causal effects.
kps.d: Several inputs capture perceptions and self-assessments. DORA explicitly labels the profile names and descriptions as interpretations and warns that teams with similar measured performance may not recognise the characterisation. The supplied analysis describes associations; it does not establish that a particular intervention will move a team between profiles. Despite the report's AI-assisted development framing, this material does not isolate AI's contribution to the observed outcomes.

vlens.an: The supplied legal-tech-vendor source directly supports the proposition that software-delivery performance cannot be defined by speed alone. The DORA report’s main reason is diagnostic: throughput or deployment-frequency results do not reveal whether technical debt, inefficient processes, instability or burnout produced them, so delivery must be assessed alongside reliability, product value, effectiveness, friction and burnout. It also supports differentiated intervention by describing distinct combinations of constraints rather than prescribing a uniform acceleration strategy. Material variation lies within the report’s archetypes: fast and stable delivery can coincide with either average or low burnout and friction, while slower delivery can still be valuable and sustainable; conversely, high-impact work can be operationally unstable. The report also limits the force of its findings by presenting the archetypes as interpretive, descriptive reference points rather than definitive diagnoses or evidence that AI caused the observed outcomes. Because the curated evidence contains one source, this establishes that source’s position, not the prevalence of this view among legal-tech vendors generally.

elens.an: The 2025 DORA report directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition that software-delivery performance cannot be defined by speed alone. Its survey-based cluster analysis evaluates throughput and instability alongside product value, team and individual effectiveness, friction and burnout, because similar delivery metrics may arise from materially different technical, process or workforce constraints. It also supports differentiated intervention: unstable legacy systems, inefficient processes and foundational gaps produce distinct performance profiles rather than a single problem remediable through a uniform push for greater speed. Material internal variation reinforces rather than weakens this position. Some profiles combine high throughput with stability, challenging an inevitable speed–stability trade-off; another combines lower throughput with positive value, reliability and working conditions, showing that slower delivery is not necessarily poor performance. Even the two strong-delivery profiles differ in burnout and friction. The report nevertheless limits the inference that can be drawn: its archetypes are interpretive descriptions, some measures are perceptual or self-assessed, and the evidence does not isolate AI as the cause of the observed outcomes. As the supplied material contains one curated source, this assessment characterises that source only and does not indicate the prevalence of this view among 2025 publications.
